thread.title: Netflix: Foreign Sign-Up Tests Could Point Toward a Solid Q3

author: David Marino-Nachison
title: Netflix: Foreign Sign-Up Tests Could Point Toward a Solid Q3
text:
Photo: LIONEL BONAVENTURE/AFP/Getty Images 12:10 p.m. ET Recent reports that Netflix (NFLX) is testing ways to bypass Apple ’s (AAPL) app store overseas indicates the possibility of solid foreign subscribers growth in addition to boosted sales and profits, according to a Thursday report from Imperial Capital.
The background: A number of stories from the business and tech press indicating that in several foreign markets, the Barron’s Next 50 company is testing a way to keep people who sign up via iOS from going through the app store. TechCrunch has a take that explains this in more detail .
That, naturally, could mean more money for Netflix and less for Apple; the equation might come down to whether the extra work for consumers has an effect on sales. (For more on international subscribers and Netflix, revisit Tiernan Ray’s take from April .)
Newsletter Sign-up Imperial, which didn’t change its “outperform” rating or $494 share price target, figures Netflix wouldn't do this if business in those markets wasn’t good. (A Bloomberg story took a higher-altitude look at the issue of companies seeking to pay lower app store “taxes.”)
“We simply have a tough time believing that Netflix would ‘experiment’ with billing infrastructure mid-quarter if it did not believe that its international subscriber levels were trending ahead of guidance,” Imperial’s analysts wrote.
 With that in mind, they boosted their Q3 estimates for subscribers and revenue slightly—and set their EPS estimate to $0.70, ahead of the company’s $0.68 guidance. (We took a look at another bullish analyst’s take on Netflix yesterday.)
Netflix “might be more willing to take the chance of creating a little bit more ‘friction’ in exchange for more substantial return,” they wrote. “As such, the experiment is not a surprise in that Netflix consistently sees its platform as ‘beautifully imperfect,’ and is always looking for ways to tweak the service.”
